title: No-Vacation Nation: Comparing the US to Other Wealthy Nations
author: John Schmitt
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2025/09/IMG_2191-680x510.jpeg)

Photograph by Nathaniel St. Clair

The United States is the only rich, democratic country in the world that does
not guarantee workers the right to paid vacation. As a result, 23 percent of
the US civilian workforce — or about 33 million workers — lack any paid
vacation, and the amount that employers provide voluntarily — an average of 10
days per year — falls well below even the legal minimum required in almost all
comparable world economies.[1](https://cepr.net/publications/no-vacation-
nation-comparing-the-us-to-other-wealthy-nations/#fn1)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-05-at-1.05.03-PM-680x981.png)

**Figure 1** summarizes the most recent available data on the legally required
minimum annual vacation days across the rich, democratic countries that are
members of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development
(OECD).[2](https://cepr.net/publications/no-vacation-nation-comparing-the-us-
to-other-wealthy-nations/#fn2) Twenty-five of the countries require employers
to provide at least 20 paid vacation days per year. Four of these set the
minimum at 25. The minimum in the United Kingdom is 28 days per year. The
legal minimum in the remaining five countries in the figure is somewhat lower:
Korea (15), Mexico (12), Israel (12), Japan (10), and Canada
(10).[3](https://cepr.net/publications/no-vacation-nation-comparing-the-us-to-
other-wealthy-nations/#fn3)

However, uniquely among OECD countries, the legal minimum in the United States
is zero. In the absence of a legal requirement, private-sector employers, on
average, provide only 10 days of paid vacation per year.

The legally required minimum days of paid vacation in the countries in Figure
1 apply to all workers — regardless of part-time or full-time status, pay
level, or employer-size. By contrast, access to voluntarily provided paid
vacation in the United States is highly unequal (**Figure 2**). Low-wage
workers are far less likely than higher wage workers to have employer-provided
vacation. More than half (57 percent) of the lowest-paid 10 percent of workers
have no paid vacation. For workers in the bottom quarter of earnings, 43
percent have zero paid vacation days. Even at higher wages, the share without
paid vacation is not small. Fifteen percent of workers in the top 10 percent
have no employer-provided paid vacation. Part-time workers and workers in
small firms are also far less likely than full-time workers or workers in
larger firms to have employer-provided paid vacation.
